title: The Raven and the Fox — Class 6 CBSE English
subject: English

slides.title: The Raven and the Fox
bullets: Class 6 — CBSE English
Poorvi · Chapter 2 · Aesop's fable
slides.speaker_notes: A short, sharp fable from Aesop. Read with rhythm — the poem is a treat.

slides.title: What you'll be able to do
bullets: Retell the fable in your own words.
Explain how the fox tricks the raven.
Use new vocabulary correctly.
Spot pronouns, direct speech, adverbs.
Find rhyming pairs in the poem.
slides.speaker_notes: Read each; ask which is hardest.

slides.title: Aesop and his fables
bullets: Aesop was an ancient Greek storyteller.
His fables are short, with sharp morals.
Characters are usually animals.
Each fable's purpose: teach a life lesson.
Today's fable is one of his most famous.
slides.speaker_notes: Connect to other Aesop fables students may know.

slides.title: The setup
bullets: A raven steals a piece of cheese.
He flies to a tall tree to eat it.
A hungry fox sees the cheese.
The fox cannot climb the tree.
He needs a TRICK.
slides.speaker_notes: Pause: ask 'how could a fox get a cheese from a high branch?'

slides.title: The trick — flattery
bullets: Fox: 'How beautiful you are!'
Fox: 'Your shining black feathers, your wings — heavenly!'
Fox: 'Surely a bird so beautiful must have a wonderful voice?'
Raven (full of pride) opens his beak to show off.
PLOP — the cheese falls!
slides.speaker_notes: Walk through the trick step by step.

slides.title: The moral
bullets: The fox grabs the cheese and runs.
He calls back: 'You have voice — but no SENSE!'
Moral: Beware of those who flatter you.
They often want something from you.
This is one of the oldest lessons in storytelling.
slides.speaker_notes: State the moral clearly; ask for modern examples.

slides.title: Vocabulary you should know
bullets: flatter — praise excessively (to get something).
vain — too proud of one's appearance.
pride — excessive self-importance.
cunning — clever in a sneaky way.
sense — good judgement; common sense.
slides.speaker_notes: Use each word in a sentence on the board.

slides.title: Language: pronouns
bullets: Pronouns replace nouns.
Personal pronouns: I, you, he, she, it, we, they.
Without pronouns: 'The raven saw the fox. The raven opened the raven's beak.'
With pronouns: 'The raven saw the fox. He opened HIS beak.'
Pronouns make sentences flow.
slides.speaker_notes: Show the contrast on the board.

slides.title: Language: direct speech
bullets: DIRECT SPEECH = the speaker's exact words, in quotation marks.
Format: She said, "Hello!"
Comma after 'said'; quote marks around the words; punctuation INSIDE the quotes.
Example: The fox said, "What a beautiful raven you are!"
Useful for stories and dialogues.

slides.title: Language: adverbs and rhyme
bullets: ADVERBS describe actions: quickly, sweetly, softly.
Many end in -ly (but not all — fast, soon are also adverbs).
RHYME: pairs of words sounding alike at the end.
From the poem: cheese / ease; fox / rocks; refuse / news.
Rhyme makes a poem easy to remember.

slides.title: Spot the parts
bullets: Sentence: 'The cunning fox spoke sweetly to the proud raven.'
Adjectives: cunning, proud.
Adverb: sweetly.
Common nouns: fox, raven.
Verb (past tense): spoke.

slides.title: You try (5 minutes)
bullets: 1. Why doesn't the fox just take the cheese?
2. What weakness in the raven does the fox use?
3. Find a rhyming pair from the poem.
4. Convert: 'I will sing for you' to direct speech inside quotation marks.
5. State the moral in your own words.

slides.title: Quick check
bullets: Q1. Who wrote the fable?
Q2. What is the moral?
Q3. Pronoun in 'The fox grinned at him': ?
Q4. Rhymes with 'fox'?
Show your answers on fingers.

slides.title: Key takeaways
bullets: Aesop's fable about a fox who flatters a vain raven.
The fox's trick: praise → ask raven to sing → cheese falls.
Moral: BEWARE OF FLATTERERS — they often want something.
Vocabulary: flatter, vain, pride, cunning, sense.
Pronouns replace nouns; direct speech uses quotation marks.
Adverbs often end in -ly; poems use RHYME.
slides.speaker_notes: Hand out worksheet; announce the write-your-own-fable homework.
